transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-15
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Patel (CTO - Solara), Evan Brooks (ML Eng - Solara), Sofia Mendes (Head of Security), Tom Wu (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
- Solara is evaluating Redwood for a mix of hosted + dedicated, with potential private deployment for regulated data.
- Key concerns: context length (32k vs 128k), multilingual support (ES/BR/JP), tool-calling for internal APIs, and cost/latency tradeoffs.
- SE agreed to run context-length perf tests and share results; security to schedule deeper review.

Topics: model selection, context windows, tool-calling, deployment modes (hosted/dedicated/private), security/compliance

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone thanks for joining, really appreciate you squeezing this in. Quick roll call and then we'll jump into what you care about.
[00:10] Priya (CTO): Hi Maya, Priya here. Evan, Sofia, Tom are on from Solara.
[00:15] Evan: Hey all.
[00:17] Sofia: Hi.
[00:18] Diego (SE): Diego from Redwood, happy to go deep on perf and models.
[00:22] Maya: Cool. Priya, can you give a 2-minute background on Solara's use case so we can orient the model discussion?
[00:30] Priya: Yeah, sure. We're a retail insights platform, we ingest POS and returns data plus customer reviews, a lot of free text. The main product is a generative insights assistant for merchants — explain trends, produce weekly summaries, and power a search-like assistant for merchants and internal ops. We're multi-region, most customers in NA and LATAM, some JP customers. Key constraints: lowish latency for the assistant (target p95 under 400ms for short queries), accurate bilingual Spanish/Portuguese output, and we have a few customers that need long-context analyses like multi-day threads and full-month logs — that's where context window becomes a big question. Also security: some vendors want dedicated/on-prem due to PII retention laws.
[01:12] Maya: Great, that helps. A couple quick questions — what volume are you expecting? tokens per month, concurrency?
[01:20] Tom (Product): For the initial pilot maybe 5M tokens/month, spikes with daily reports at month-end; concurrency typical 20-30, but some batch jobs will want larger throughput. If pilot goes well, could scale to 100M tokens/month.
[01:34] Diego: Helpful. On the model side, are you leaning open models or do you want managed LLMs?
[01:40] Evan: We prefer open models for cost control and to avoid vendor lock, but we also need good instruction-following and tool-calling for our internal connectors. Latency matters too.
[01:48] Maya: Perfect — that's exactly the sweet spot for Redwood. We support hosted API with curated open models, our Dedicated pools for committed throughput, and Private (VPC) for customers that need full network isolation and KMS integration.
[02:00] Priya: Can you unpack recommended model families? We're evaluating Mistral, Llama-2/3 derivatives, MPT, and some of the newest 70B/100B open variants. Also curious about quantized variants for cost.
[02:12] Diego: Sure. High level: smaller 7–13B families are great for lower-cost, higher-concurrency and many classification tasks. For more complex summarization and multi-turn reasoning, 33B–70B models tend to give better coherence. The larger 70B+ are good if you need nuanced reasoning with very long context, but cost and latency rise. For multilingual Spanish/Portuguese/Japanese support, we've seen Mistral variants and some Llama-3 forks do well, but results vary — we recommend evals on your prompts.
[02:45] Evan: What about context windows? We have some prompts that need 32k, others that might need 100k-ish for archive summarization.
[02:52] Diego: Redwood supports models with different context lengths. Practically, we can route requests to a 32k context variant for most calls and to a 128k or custom long-context variant for archival jobs. For hosted, we have a set of verified 32k and 128k open models; for Dedicated you can pin model binaries and we can host your long-context builds. Private gives you even more flexibility to bring a custom kernel/compile. A couple caveats: longer contexts increase per-token latency and memory pressure — we do continuous batching and prefix caching to mitigate cost.
[03:25] Priya: When you say prefix caching, is that the same as KV cache? We've tried some vendors with poor cache invalidation.
[03:31] Diego: Right, it's our KV cache and prefix caching. We automatic prefix cache often for repeated system prompts and docs; we also expose controls so you can tune TTLs. Sometimes transcripts will say K V cash in the transcript — ignore the noise.
[03:41] Sofia: From a security standpoint, how does key management work? We need CMEK/HSM integration and audit logs for every inference.
[03:49] Maya: For Private deployments we integrate customer KMS/HSM for encryption at rest and in-transit. We surface audit logs (per request metadata) and retention policies. For Dedicated we also support customer-managed key rotations — we'll share the SOC2 and architecture docs.
[04:02] Sofia: OK we'll need the SOC 2 Type II evidence and a network architecture diagram. Also SSO/SAML support and RBAC.
[04:10] Maya: Absolutely — I'll attach the security pack and we can schedule a security deep dive.
[04:15] Evan: Diego, can you talk a bit about tool-calling? We need the model to call internal connectors: inventory API, promotions service, and a custom python microservice for calculations. We want structured JSON outputs and safe sandboxing.
[04:28] Diego: Sure. We support two types: built-in function/tool-calling hooks that allow models to emit a structured JSON payload which your orchestration layer can parse; and external tool-chains where we call your service via a secure outbound connection (on Private/VPC) or via a broker in Dedicated/Hosted with OAuth. You can define strict schemas so the model only outputs allowed fields. For sandboxing, we recommend function-first pattern: model returns a func call, your system executes, and then optionally the model gets the result to continue.
[04:55] Tom: Any limitations on number of tool calls per request or latency implications?
[04:59] Diego: Each external call adds round-trip latency; our routing can batch internal calls where sensible. For high QPS tool-calling workflows we often suggest asynchronous job patterns or pre-fetching relevant doc contexts to avoid repeated calls. We can also cache tool outputs if they are idempotent.
[05:16] Priya: Can Redwood host a custom Llama-3 quantized 4-bit build in Dedicated? We want to squeeze cost but keep quality.
[05:23] Diego: Yes, Dedicated is designed for that. We can take your quantized weights, run the compile and optimized kernels, then validate memory/latency. For extreme cost optimization we also suggest Redwood Optimize recommendations — e.g., mix-precision, dynamic batching, and caching. There are tradeoffs though: very aggressive quantization can hit hallucination rates for certain tasks.
[05:45] Evan: Speaking of hallucinations and quality control — how do you do evals and regression detection?
[05:49] Maya: We have built-in evaluation harnesses where you can upload prompt sets and expected outputs; Redwood runs nightly/eval jobs and can alert on quality regressions tied to model updates or quantization changes. You can tie alerts to rollbacks or canary policies.
[06:03] Priya: For our pilot we'd like to compare 33B Llama-3 fork vs Mistral-70B-v1 across our prompt set at both 32k and 128k. Can Diego run that?
[06:13] Diego: Yes — I've noted that as an action. We'll run latency, p95, cost per 1k tokens, and a set of QA metrics (BLEU-ish / factuality checks) and share a CSV.
[06:24] Sofia: Also need to confirm data residency — some LATAM partners require data stored in region. Can Redwood pin region for hosted?
[06:31] Maya: Hosted can be region pinned depending on model availability; Dedicated and Private give you firm controls. We'll include region options in the pricing sheet.
[06:40] Tom: Regarding deployment rollout — can we do canary and A/B tests across model variants?
[06:45] Diego: Yes, Redwood Console has rollout features: canary percentages, automatic fallback policies, and per-route model pins. You can segment by token type or route. We also expose per-token cost breakdowns in Console.
[06:58] Evan: What's the typical time to get Dedicated set up? We're worried about a long lead time.
[07:02] Maya: For reserved Dedicated capacity typical lead time is 2–4 weeks for standard configurations; if you're bringing custom kernels or on-prem hardware it can be longer. For pilot we recommend starting on Hosted with Verified models to get early feedback while we spin up Dedicated nodes.
[07:17] Priya: That sounds sensible. Cost-wise, do you provide sim models for us to estimate unit economics?
[07:23] Diego: We provide per-token unit costs for model families plus an estimate for infra costs. We'll also produce a simulated cost spreadsheet using your token profile — that's part of the action.
[07:33] Priya: One more — multilingual fidelity. We've had poor Portuguese outputs from some Llama variants. Any specific recommendations?
[07:39] Diego: We've seen Mistral x multilingual forks and some Llama-3 specialized weights perform better. The only reliable approach is to run your prompts through both families. We'll include language-level metrics in the eval CSV.
[07:52] Tom: About tools and security: if we want the model to call internal APIs, can we require mutual TLS from Redwood to our connector?
[07:58] Maya: On Private/VPC yes. For Dedicated we can set up mutual TLS or token-based auth via a secure broker. For Hosted we typically use OAuth/brokered connections, but we can discuss custom arrangements for enterprise.
[08:12] Sofia: We'll want a whiteboard session with your infra security team to review network diagrams and the KMS flow.
[08:18] Maya: We'll set that up.
[08:20] Evan: Are there any gotchas with long-context tokenization or costs when you combine retrieval with 128k contexts?
[08:27] Diego: Two gotchas: first, naive retrieval that passes whole documents into the prompt increases token bills — better to do chunking and extractive summarization to reduce context. Second, some older model kernels have quadratic attention costs; our runtime picks optimized kernels or sliding-window attention for very long contexts. We'll share notes on best practices.
[08:47] Priya: Good. For the pilot timeline we want to start in January. We're aiming for pilot success criteria: <500ms median latency on short queries, multilingual accuracy >90 on curated prompts, and 25% lower cost than current vendor.
[09:04] Maya: That's clear — we'll map actions to those criteria.
[09:08] Diego: Quick note: for evals please provide the redacted prompts and expected outputs; if you have scoring rubrics share those too.
[09:15] Priya: Will do.
[09:18] Maya: Alright, let's recap next steps — I'll send the security pack and pricing, Diego will run the 32k/128k tests, Priya will upload prompts, and we'll schedule the security deep dive. Anything else?
[09:31] Tom: Could you include a sample of the Console dashboards — latency breakdown and per-route cost?
[09:36] Maya: Yes, will attach screenshots and a quick video.
[09:38] Sofia: Also include the SOC2 artifacts and the network diagram.
[09:40] Maya: Noted.
[09:42] Priya: Thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[09:44] Maya: Thanks, we'll follow up with notes and the sheet.
[09:47] End meeting.
